In Release 18, NR conducted a comprehensive analysis of inter-gNB interference management, resulting in the specification of several mitigation schemes for Release 19. A key technique among these is the exchange of CSI-RS/SSB information to enable gNB-gNB channels and interference measurements, which is vital for identifying both aggressor and victim gNBs. This facilitates spatial mitigation measures, including Tx/Rx beam nulling and the identification of the most interfering downlink beams. Furthermore, exchanging information about the 6G frame structure will support coordinated scheduling across gNBs. For 6G, RAN1 should use these information exchanges as a foundational approach. Proposal 9. For network-side interference mitigation, 6G to consider at least information exchange of 6G RS for channel/interference measurements, strongest beams and exchange of 6G frame structure time and frequency configurations. Additionally, to enable efficient interference mitigation, RAN1 should study mechanism for information exchange of inter-gNB channel and CLI report/feedback. Proposal 10. For network-side interference mitigation, RAN1 to study mechanism for CLI reporting and feedback.

Hierarchical Framework for Special Scenarios The agreement in section 1 mandates the consideration of scenarios beyond single cell/carrier/TRP, such as NTN, SBFD, multi-carrier, and multi-TRP. To prevent the fragmentation of the RACH specification, RAN1 should adopt a "Baseline + Delta" methodology. The foundational RACH procedure and formats should be designed to support the terrestrial (TN) baseline scenario. For specialized deployments like NTN or SBFD, the study should exclusively focus on identifying necessary "special handling" or delta modifications (e.g., tolerance for large frequency offsets for NTN, or specific interference mitigation for SBFD) that can be applied on top of the unified baseline, rather than developing standalone access procedures. Proposal 3: Adopt a "Baseline + Delta" design approach where a unified RACH framework is established for the baseline TN scenario, and specialized scenarios (NTN, SBFD, multi-carrier, multi-TRP) are supported strictly through specific functional enhancements (delta) applied to the baseline.

In RAN1#122, consensus was reached that studies focus on identifying technical aspects impacted by NTN characteristics, with attention to lessons learned from NR and IoT NTN. Harmonization in the context of 6G should be interpreted as the creation of a single and efficient framework, where TN serve as the baseline foundation. TN will continue to be the primary deployment scenario and the main driver of performance and scalability. For this reason, the baseline framework must be optimized around TN operation, ensuring that performance and simplicity are not compromised. NTN can then be introduced as scalable extensions that interoperate with the TN baseline, rather than imposing structural changes on the fundamental design from the outset. Harmonization, therefore, is not the act of embedding every NTN-specific requirement into the baseline but rather the establishment of an adaptable architecture. Such an approach allows NTN to be incorporated in a flexible, consistent manner while safeguarding the stability, efficiency, and integrity of TN operation. From a feature perspective, the starting point should be a compact TN baseline feature set, rather than an extensive and pre-defined catalog of NTN requirements. This approach avoids unnecessary complexity and ensures that the core framework remains streamlined. Any potential NTN features should be subject to clear and strict criteria: they must be implementable as minimal add-ons that do not degrade TN performance, do not increase operational complexity, and do not introduce unintended limitations. NTN support in this model is envisioned as general, lightweight, and non-intrusive, so that integration can occur without undermining TN deployment. At the same time, certain fundamental aspects must be acknowledged. In particular, considerations for time and frequency compensation represent essential elements, as these are inherent to NTN operation and unavoidable in a harmonized framework. However, beyond such foundational elements, feature-specific optimizations targeting NTN should be postponed at this stage, to prevent the premature inclusion of niche-driven requirements that risk overcomplicating the baseline. Proposal #26: Consider a TN-centric 6G baseline, with NTN supported only through minimal, scalable extensions. The focus should remain on preserving TN performance and simplicity, while limiting NTN features to essential aspects such as time/frequency compensation.

{"chunk_id":"R1-2601879-003","collection":"ran1_tdoc_chunks","metadata":{"source":["Kyocera Corporation"],"tdocNumber":"R1-2601879","title":"Beam management for downlink and uplink"},"point_id":"3106431802391076561"}
tion framework to support mTRP beam indication, including the design space of a unified TCI framework that involves joint and separate DL/UL TCI state(s) for mTRP while considering sTRP as a special case. When there is a mismatch between the beamwidth of the TCI state reference signal and the target signal, it can necessitate multiple TCI state switches, resulting in increased signaling overhead. Hence, the design of the 6G QCL framework should address the issue of frequent TCI state switching, identifying this as a key area for further investigation. Study mechanisms within the QCL/TCI framework to alleviate frequent TCI switching (including cases where QCL source RS beamwidth differs from the target signal beamwidth). Moreover, it is also important to explore simplified QCL chains for 6G beam indication. For example: Evaluating the removal of TRS as a QCL source involves considering how essential TRS is for beam indication and whether its functions could be replaced or streamlined to reduce complexity and overhead. TRS is typically used to provide channel state information for accurate beamforming and alignment, but its periodic transmission can contribute to significant signalling and processing burden, especially in scenarios with frequent beam switching or where multiple reference signals are involved. By exploring the possibility of removing TRS from the QCL chain, the aim is to simplify the reference signal structure, potentially relying more heavily on other reference signals, which may offer similar benefits with reduced overhead. This approach requires a thorough assessment of any potential impacts on channel estimation accuracy and overall system performance, as well as the feasibility of maintaining robust beam management without TRS. Examining low-latency beam indication methods is crucial for supporting fast and efficient beam switching, especially in highly dynamic scenarios such as high-mobility users or dense mTRP deployments. Prediction-based techniques, for example, involve forecasting the optimal beam direction based on historical measurements, mobility patterns, or environmental context. These techniques can leverage AI/ML algorithms to enhance prediction accuracy, adapt to complex scenarios, and reduce the signalling required for beam updates. Alternatively, non-AI approaches might use deterministic algorithms or statistical models to predict beam changes with minimal computational overhead. Supporting both AI/ML and non-AI/ML methods ensures flexibility and adaptability to different deployment conditions and device capabilities, ultimately aiming to achieve lower latency, reduced signalling, and improved user experience in 6G radio access networks. Study a streamlined QCL property/chain design for 6GR beam indication that evaluates reducing or removing reliance on UE-specific periodic TRS as a QCL source RS with an explicit assessment of impacts on tracking/channel estimation robustness, system performance, and overhead/energy consumption; and investigates low-latency beam indication mechanisms to support fast beam/TRP switching, including prediction-assisted indication methods that can be realized with AI/ML as well as non-AI approaches, with the objective of reducing signaling and beam update latency in dynamic (e.g., high mobility and dense mTRP) deployments.

Ultimately, this ensures a holistic and accurate evaluation of energy efficiency. Observation 2: The modeling approaches and principles from the 5G NR energy saving studies can be reused along with existing metrics as much as possible. Proposal 3: RAN1 should focus on revising the evaluation methodology for 6GR energy savings to accommodate relevant scenarios, novel technologies like AI and ISAC, and the increased flexibility provided by the foundational design aspects like initial access. Since power consumption is primarily scaled with the use of resources in transmission/reception, in time, spatial, bandwidth and transmit-power domain, the classification of the energy saving techniques into these domains should be adopted and will be beneficial. Likewise, the evaluations of energy saving gains as well as impact to network and user performance can be the basic approach by reusing existing KPIs whenever applicable and introducing new KPIs as needed. Once a revised version of the 6GR power saving evaluation methodology, including power consumption models and KPIs are finalized, all relevant agenda items should employ them for evaluation. Once a revised version of the 6GR power saving evaluation methodology, including power consumption models and KPIs are finalized, all relevant agenda items should employ them for evaluation. Proposal 4: Once a revised version of the 6GR power saving evaluation methodology, including the power consumption models and KPIs are finalized, all relevant agenda items should employ them for evaluation.

{"chunk_id":"R1-2603171-006","collection":"ran1_tdoc_chunks","metadata":{"source":["ITL"],"tdocNumber":"R1-2603171","title":"PRACH and RACH procedure for 6GR"},"point_id":"10313289926191812404"}
undational procedure for 6GR random access. To minimize specification fragmentation and reduce UE and gNB implementation complexity, the legacy 4-step RACH procedure should be adopted as the definitive baseline. While 2-step RACH and RACH-less procedures offer theoretical latency reduction and resource efficiency, their applicability is heavily scenario-dependent. Therefore, rather than defining them as co-baselines, 2-step and RACH-less operations should be treated as conditional enhancements. Future studies should focus on identifying the specific deployment scenarios (e.g., ultra-low latency requirements or specific RRC sub-state transitions) where the introduction of these alternative procedures provides justifiable gains over the 4-step baseline. Proposal 15: Adopt the 4-step RACH procedure as the sole baseline for 6GR. 2-step RACH and RACH-less procedures should be studied as conditional enhancements applicable only to specific, justified scenarios. To support aggressive Network Energy Savings (NES) and reduce initial access latency, the RACH procedure should not rely solely on UE-initiated attempts. Dynamic network-controlled triggering mechanisms should be structurally integrated. Specifically, the framework should support PDCCH order and Paging-triggered Contention-Free Random Access (CFRA). By allowing the gNB to dynamically allocate CFRA resources to a paged UE, the network can eliminate contention delays and avoid the inefficient, permanent reservation of CFRA resources. The procedural timelines and DCI/Paging payload designs required to support this dynamic triggering should be prioritized in upcoming RAN1 meetings. Proposal 16: Support dynamic, network-controlled RACH triggering mechanisms, specifically focusing on PDCCH order and Paging-triggered CFRA, to optimize resource utilization and reduce access latency. The concept of "early indication" via Msg1 requires strict demarcation to prevent overlapping with RAN2 MAC/RRC functions. Transmitting actual data payloads within Msg1 introduces excessive complexity and contradicts the physical purpose of the preamble. Consequently, early indication in Msg1 should be strictly limited to L1 signaling mechanisms, such as sequence selection or preamble partitioning. The study should focus exclusively on how these physical layer mechanisms can indicate UE intentions (e.g., slicing requirements, RedCap capabilities) to the gNB prior to Msg2/Msg3, without altering the fundamental waveform structure. Proposal 17: Restrict Msg1 early indication strictly to physical layer mechanisms, such as preamble partitioning or sequence selection, and explicitly exclude the transmission of data payloads within Msg1. The 5G NR approach to coverage enhancement suffers from fragmented, per-message repetition configurations, which increases signaling overhead and UE implementation complexity. For 6GR, a unified coverage enhancement framework that spans the entire initial access procedure (Msg1 through Msg5) should be established. RAN1 should study joint repetition configuration mechanisms where a single network indication (e.g., via SIB or a unified DCI) can dictate the repetition factors and combining schemes for all associated physical channels in the RACH sequence. Proposal 18: Establish a unified coverage enhancement framework that jointly configures and manages repetition schemes across the entire RACH procedure (Msg1 to Msg5) to reduce signaling overhead and implementation complexity.
